1	Benchmark contamination is widely assumed to inflate language model scores, yet the actual effect has never been systematically measured across model families. We perform controlled SFT injection at five dosage levels into six models spanning five independent families (7B--14.7B parameters) and discover that contamination produces not one effect but a spectrum of dose-response patterns. Benefit ($+$2.4pp mean) and Immune ($\Delta < 1$\,percentage point [pp]) are replicated across independent families (three and two, respectively); more extreme responses---catastrophic collapse ($-$9 to $-$25pp across seeds) and V-recovery---are each observed in one family (Qwen2.5) across three seeds, requiring further replication. Counter-intuitively, the 14B Qwen model is 3$\times$ more fragile than 7B. These effects are benchmark-conditional: models harmed on MMLU can simultaneously benefit on GSM8K ($+$11pp), revealing asymmetric cross-benchmark transfer. Difference-in-differences analysis finds no item-specific memorization on MMLU (minimum detectable effect size 1.2--2.0pp); ARC has limited power (2.3--5.6pp). Profiles are robust: within-seed bootstrap stability exceeds 99.6\% for 4/5 MMLU families, though cross-seed sign consistency is 3/6. Out-of-sample validation on a held-out sixth family (LLaMA-3.1-8B) confirms the profiles generalize: it is classified Immune despite a baseline matching OLMo-2's Benefit, showing that model family characteristics beyond baseline ability modulate vulnerability. file.content: Benchmark contamination is widely assumed to inflate language model scores, yet the actual effect has never been systematically measured across model families. We perform controlled SFT injection at five dosage levels into six models spanning five independent families (7B--14.7B parameters) and discover that contamination produces not one effect but a spectrum of dose-response patterns. Benefit ($+$2.4pp mean) and Immune ($\Delta < 1$\,percentage point [pp]) are replicated across independent families (three and two, respectively); more extreme responses---catastrophic collapse ($-$9 to $-$25pp across seeds) and V-recovery---are each observed in one family (Qwen2.5) across three seeds, requiring further replication. In our six-family sample, contamination vulnerability concentrates in the 65--70\% MMLU baseline band; models at extreme baselines show limited sensitivity. Counter-intuitively, the 14B Qwen model is 3$\times$ more fragile than 7B. These effects are benchmark-conditional: MMLU-targeted contamination universally improves GSM8K ($+$1 to $+$16pp across all tested families), even in models harmed on MMLU, providing converging evidence for capability elicitation rather than item memorization. Difference-in-differences analysis finds no item-specific memorization on MMLU (minimum detectable effect size 1.2--2.0pp); ARC has limited power (2.3--5.6pp). Profiles are robust: within-seed bootstrap stability exceeds 99.6\% for 4/5 MMLU families, cross-seed direction agreement reaches 5/6, though strict sign consistency is 3/6. ARC-Challenge achieves 4/5 directional agreement despite its smaller item pool (1{,}172 vs.\ 14{,}042 items). We characterize contamination detection signal failure: Min-K\%++ exhibits directional reversal at small scales (paired Cohen's $d = -1.98$ at d100; $|d| > 1.4$ at d005), actively misleading practitioners. Simulation establishes that IRT-based contamination diagnosis requires ensemble sizes ($J \geq 50$) above current practice. Out-of-sample validation on a held-out sixth family (LLaMA-3.1-8B) confirms the profiles generalize: it is classified Immune despite a baseline matching OLMo-2's Benefit, showing that model family characteristics beyond baseline ability modulate vulnerability. Our findings demonstrate that ``contamination equals inflation'' masks substantial heterogeneity; model-specific dose-response profiling is necessary for reliable benchmark interpretation.
